noop_method.title: String methods don't change the original — they return a new value
noop_method.bank_description: Student believes that calling a string method (such as .upper(), .lower(), .strip(), .replace(), or .split()) modifies the original string variable in place, like list.append() does.
noop_method.contrast_code:
name = "hello"
name.upper()
print(name)          # student expects "HELLO"

# Fix: capture the return value
name = name.upper()
print(name)          # now prints "HELLO"
steps: Strings in Python are immutable — they can never be changed in place.
Methods like .upper() create and RETURN a brand-new string; the original variable is untouched unless you assign the result back.
Write  name = name.upper()  (capture the return value) instead of just  name.upper()  (which discards it).
noop_method.takeaway: Every string method returns a new string — always assign the result if you want to keep it.

range_1_to_n.title: range(n) starts at 0, not 1 — and stops before n
range_1_to_n.bank_description: Student believes that range(n) produces the sequence 1, 2, ..., n (like a 1-based count), when it actually produces 0, 1, ..., n-1.
steps: range(n) always starts at 0 — the first value is 0, not 1.
range(n) stops BEFORE n — it never includes n itself.
To get 1 through n use range(1, n+1).  To get k through m-1 use range(k, m).
range_1_to_n.takeaway: range(n) gives you exactly n numbers: 0, 1, 2, ..., n-1.

index_1_based.title: Python lists and strings start at index 0, not 1
index_1_based.bank_description: Student believes the first element of a list or string is at index 1, so a[1] is the first element, a[2] is the second, and so on.
index_1_based.contrast_code:
a = [10, 20, 30]
print(a[0])   # 10  — the FIRST element
print(a[1])   # 20  — the SECOND element
print(a[2])   # 30  — the THIRD element
steps: Python uses 0-based indexing: the very first element is always at index 0.
a[1] is the SECOND element, a[2] is the THIRD, and so on.
To access the first element write a[0]; the last element of a length-n list is at a[n-1] (or a[-1]).
index_1_based.takeaway: Index 0 = first element. Index 1 = second. Always subtract 1 from your intuition.

assign_copies.title: Assigning a list variable creates an alias, not a copy
assign_copies.bank_description: Student believes that writing b = a creates an independent copy of the list stored in a, so later changes to a do not affect b.
assign_copies.contrast_code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a          # b is an ALIAS — same list in memory
a.append(4)
print(b)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]  — b sees the change too

# To make an independent copy:
b = a.copy()   # or b = list(a) or b = a[:]
a.append(5)
print(b)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]  — unchanged
steps: In Python, lists are objects stored in memory.  b = a copies the REFERENCE (address), not the data — both names now point to the same list.
Any mutation through either name (a.append, b.pop, etc.) affects the single shared list.
To get an independent copy use a.copy(), list(a), or a[:].
assign_copies.takeaway: b = a makes two names for one list. Use b = a.copy() to get two separate lists.

add_before_div.title: Python follows standard operator precedence: * and / before + and -
add_before_div.bank_description: Student believes that addition (+) is evaluated before division (/), so  a + b / c  is computed as  (a + b) / c  instead of  a + (b / c).
add_before_div.contrast_code:
print(10 + 20 / 2)    # 20.0  NOT 15.0
#  Python evaluates: 10 + (20 / 2) = 10 + 10.0 = 20.0
#  Student expects:  (10 + 20) / 2 = 30 / 2   = 15.0

# Use parentheses to force the order you want:
print((10 + 20) / 2)  # 15.0
steps: Python (like maths) evaluates * and / BEFORE + and -, so  a + b / c  means  a + (b / c).
If you want addition first, use explicit parentheses: (a + b) / c.
When in doubt, add parentheses — they make the intent clear and prevent bugs.
add_before_div.takeaway: Division binds tighter than addition. Write (a+b)/c if you mean that.
